released: not yet: the v2.0.0rc4 tag's own creation date, to be filled in when the tag is cut. The tag does not exist in this repository yet, so there is nothing to record here -- and a date written before the tag existed would be one that never happened.
released_as: not yet: the commit the v2.0.0rc4 tag will point at, to be filled in when the tag is cut. Left empty on purpose rather than guessed. Every other released_as in this directory names a commit that is in this repository and can be checked with git; a plausible-looking hash here would be the one entry that could not be, and 1.1.0.json's entire argument is that the commit is the part that has to be real. Two fields are to be filled in at that moment and only these two: released and released_as.
why_there_is_no_record: Not measured, and this is a rehearsal like the three before it. rc4 exists because rc3 shipped a binary that announced the wrong version. rc3's build succeeded on all three platforms and the release job -- the one that first failed at rc2 with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml' -- ran through and created the Release page, so the whole tag-to-Release-page path completed for the first time. What it did not do was carry the version the tag named: a build reads its version from pyproject.toml and not from the tag, the tree was not bumped in the same step the tag was cut, and pyproject.toml still read 2.0.0rc2 at v2.0.0rc3. So the tag and the Release page announced 2.0.0rc3 while the binary inside them announced 2.0.0rc2. rc4 is cut from a tree whose version sources all read 2.0.0rc4, so that this candidate -- the first one -- ships as one version instead of two. No sweep runs at this tag either: benchmarks/perf_baseline.py and benchmarks/compare/run_comparison.py are not executed at an rc, for the reason 1.2.1.json gives.
the_guard_that_was_supposed_to_catch_it_: This is not a bug that was found and fixed; it is the check doing what it was built for, the first time it was exercised. 2.0.0rc2 added test_the_tag_at_head_names_the_version_this_build_reports to tests/unit/test_version.py, and the reason it gives in its own docstring is this exact accident: pyproject.toml is what the metadata and the frozen binary's file properties carry, the tag reaches the pipeline only as a ref cut by a separate step, and a tag cut without the bump ships a binary, a release page and a tag that disagree while every check comparing the notes against gigaxml.__version__ passes. At v2.0.0rc3 the version was not bumped, and that test failed on all five legs of test.yml with the tag and the tree side by side: the tag 'v2.0.0rc3' at HEAD names version '2.0.0rc3', but pyproject.toml says '2.0.0rc2'. The three platform builds and the release job had already gone green by then, which is the point -- the packaging pipeline cannot see this defect, and a released binary was already downloadable before the tag guard was read. The guard has nothing to prove at rc4: it passes here because the tree and the tag agree, and it will be the check that fails if the bump is ever skipped again.
how_this_differs_from_the_three_before_i: All four entries are recorded: false, and the four absences are not the same absence, so this file says which one it is rather than letting a reader infer it. rc1's build died on all three platforms and produced no artifact at all, so there was nothing that could have been measured even in principle -- any figure in that file would have described a binary that does not exist. rc2's build succeeded and produced three downloadable artifacts, and the release job one step later failed, so the tag has artifacts and no Release page; the measurement was simply never taken. rc3's build and release assembly both completed, so the tag has a Release page for the first time, and the version it shipped under was wrong -- the measurement was again not taken. rc4's version sources are all in agreement, so it is the first candidate that could be published as the single release it claims to be; the measurement is still not taken, because a rehearsal is not a measurement point and a sweep at a version nobody installs would put a number in this directory that describes a commit rather than a release.
the_evidence_this_entry_waits_on: The v2.0.0rc4 tag's own packaging run, once the tag is cut. Until then there is no run to cite and no result to report, so this entry cites none: released and released_as above are left in the not-yet form on purpose, and the two of them are what a person fills in from git log -1 --format=%aI v2.0.0rc4 and git rev-parse v2.0.0rc4 when the tag exists. The rc3 version mismatch this files is repair for is recorded in 2.0.0rc3.json, whose own released and released_as point at the tag whose binary reported the wrong version.
no_numbers_were_fabricated_here: Deliberately empty of numbers, for the reason 2.0.0rc1.json gives and one more. Nothing has been measured at this tag, so any figure would describe a run that has not happened. And nothing has even been built yet: the tag does not exist, so this entry cannot cite a byte count or a job result the way 2.0.0rc2.json can cite its own artifacts or 2.0.0rc3.json could cite a Release page. The absence here is of the same shape as rc3's, and for the same reason -- both were written before their tag was cut.
what_would_close_this: The 2.0.0 release, for the same reason 1.2.1.json gives. A release candidate is cut to rehearse the pipeline, and proving that the tree and the tag name the same version is what this tag is for; the figures that belong in this directory are the ones taken at a version somebody installs. perf_baseline.py and run_comparison.py now write schema_version, an identity block, the generated dataset's seed and digest, and every individual run's raw values, so the 2.0.0 record will be generated rather than reconstructed. Until then 2.0.0rc4's performance is unknown -- not equal to 2.0.0rc3's, 2.0.0rc2's or 2.0.0rc1's, which also have no record, and not equal to 1.1.0's, which has one taken six commits past its own tag.
